headline: Oil hit its highest since May on reports of planned US–Israeli strikes on Iran, while a tech-led stock sell-off pushed the US 10-year yield below 5%. The yen had its best day in a month.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: The dollar index slipped about 0.2% to near 101.6, close to a three-week low. A sharp fall in tech shares and war fears sent money into US government bonds, pulling the 10-year yield below 5%. Bets on a December Federal Reserve hike held up.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: since the US–Iran war began in February, high oil has kept US inflation up, and with it bets that the Federal Reserve raises rates again in December, which supports the dollar. What changed: new claims for unemployment benefits fell to 194,000 last week, near their lowest in decades, so layoffs are still rare. But in the afternoon the Nasdaq fell about 2.6% on worries that heavy AI spending won't pay off, with Meta down about 7%, while reports of planned US and Israeli strikes on Iran added to the nerves. Investors piled into US government bonds: the 10-year yield fell to about 4.95%, roughly 0.2 percentage points lower on the day. The dollar index eased to about 101.6, losing most to the yen. What it means: lower US yields make the dollar less rewarding to hold, even though the jobs data give the Fed no reason to drop a December hike. The question to keep asking: does the stock sell-off keep pulling yields down, or does strong data pull them back up?
chapters.fx: What's next: Friday's US business surveys (flash PMIs) at 8:45 AM CT and the final University of Michigan sentiment survey, with its inflation expectations, at 9:00 AM CT. The Fed's next decision is October 28; it is in its quiet period until then.
numbers: Dollar index ~101.62 (−0.2%), near a three-week low
US 10-year yield ~4.95% (about −0.2 points on the day)
Fed: Oct 28 hike ~11%; Dec hike ~90% (CME FedWatch, Oct 21; no fresh reading verified after the bond rally)

scenarios.base: If stocks steady and oil holds near $113, the dollar index stays near 101.6 into Friday's surveys.
scenarios.bull: If Friday's surveys or inflation expectations come in hot, yields climb back above 5% and the dollar firms.
scenarios.bear: If the tech sell-off spreads and bond buying continues, yields slide further and the dollar loses more ground to the yen and franc.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro ended about 0.1% lower near $1.122, recovering a little from its morning low as the dollar slipped. Euro-area consumer confidence fell more than expected, and France's borrowing costs stayed above 5% a day before Moody's reviews its credit rating.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the euro has been held back by France's budget fight and by expensive energy, which Europe imports. The European Central Bank is expected to hold on October 29 and lean toward a hike in December, because euro-area inflation is well above its 2% target. What changed: the European Commission's flash consumer confidence fell to −17.9 in October, below the −17.0 expected, as high energy bills weigh on households. France's 10-year yield stayed above 5%, and the extra it pays over Germany remained near its widest since 2011. The euro dipped below $1.12 in the morning, then climbed back to about $1.1218 as US yields fell. What it means: gloomier households and French debt worries leave the ECB less room to keep raising rates, which weighs on the euro. The question: does Moody's cut France's rating on Friday?
chapters.fx: What's next: Friday's flash business surveys for France (2:15 AM CT), Germany (2:30 AM CT) and the euro area (3:00 AM CT), then Moody's review of France after European markets close. October 27: the French parliament's vote on the budget's tax side. October 29: the ECB's decision.
numbers: France 10-year yield above 5%; gap over Germany near its widest since 2011

scenarios.bull: If Friday's business surveys beat forecasts and oil eases, December hike bets firm and the euro recovers.
scenarios.bear: If Moody's cuts France or the surveys disappoint, the French gap over Germany widens and the euro slips back under $1.12.

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: The pound ended flat near $1.340, recovering its morning dip as the dollar eased. Coming up: UK consumer confidence at 6:01 PM CT tonight and retail sales at 1:00 AM CT Friday, which decide whether a second Bank of England hike in December looks likely.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the Gulf war has pushed up energy bills, and Britain, which imports a lot of gas, has felt it more than most. Strong jobs figures and UK inflation of 3.5% for September made a Bank of England hike on November 5 close to certain. What changed: the CBI industrial survey showed factory orders falling to −32 in October, far weaker than the −20 expected. The pound dipped to about $1.3366 in the morning on war fears, then recovered to about $1.3399 as US yields fell. What it means: weak factory orders do not change November, and the pound is holding up because the Bank of England still looks set to raise rates faster than the European Central Bank. The question: is a second hike in December justified by spending figures?
chapters.fx: What's next: GfK consumer confidence at 6:01 PM CT tonight (about −14 expected), UK retail sales for September at 1:00 AM CT Friday (−0.2% expected) and flash business surveys at 3:30 AM CT. October 28: the UK budget. November 5: the Bank of England's decision.
numbers: BoE: Nov 5 hike ~99%; Dec second hike ~51%

scenarios.bull: If retail sales or the business surveys surprise higher, December hike bets rise and so does the pound.
scenarios.bear: If spending figures disappoint after the weak factory survey, December bets fade and the pound slips.

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: The yen had its best day in a month, with the dollar down about 0.8% to near ¥156.9. Falling stock markets and war fears sent investors into safe assets, and lower US yields made the yen cheaper to hold. Japan's inflation figures come at 6:30 PM CT.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the yen has been the weakest major currency, because Japan's rates are far below everyone else's and Japan pays heavily for imported energy. The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on October 30 and is increasingly expected to hike in December. What changed: the dollar fell to about ¥156.85, its biggest one-day drop since late September, as reports of planned strikes on Iran and a sharp tech sell-off on Wall Street sent investors to safety. The US 10-year yield fell about 0.2 percentage points, narrowing the gap with Japan. The yen also gained on the euro, the pound and the Australian dollar. What it means: the yen is acting as a safe haven again, but high oil still hurts Japan's trade bill. A lasting recovery still needs a Bank of Japan hike. The question: does tonight's inflation give the bank cover to move in December?
chapters.fx: What's next: Japan's national core inflation for September at 6:30 PM CT tonight (2.1% expected, up from 1.7%), then Japan's flash business surveys at 7:30 PM CT. October 29–30: the Bank of Japan's decision.
numbers: USD/JPY ~156.85 (−0.8%); biggest daily drop since late September

scenarios.bull: If inflation runs hotter or the stock sell-off deepens, the yen extends its gains toward ¥156.
scenarios.bear: If inflation comes in soft and US yields bounce, December hike bets fade and the dollar climbs back toward ¥158.

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: The franc hit a three-month high against the euro in European trading as war fears rose, and edged up against the dollar to about 0.823. That came the same day the Swiss National Bank said it no longer needs to stand ready to step into currency markets.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the Swiss franc is a safe place to park money in a crisis, but Swiss inflation is near zero, so the Swiss National Bank holds rates at 0% and a December cut is still possible. What changed: the bank's summary of its September discussion, out this morning, said the franc has become a popular currency to borrow in for carry trades, and it dropped its stronger readiness to intervene. Later, reports of planned strikes on Iran and falling stocks sent money to safety: the euro fell to about 0.92 francs, its lowest in three months, and the dollar ended near 0.8234, down about 0.1%. The yen, not the franc, led the rush to safety. What it means: the bank is not fighting the franc in either direction, so global fear sets its path. The question: does Gulf fear keep building?
chapters.fx: What's next: no Swiss data until next week. The franc moves with war headlines and stock markets. December 10: the Swiss National Bank's next decision.
numbers: SNB policy rate 0%; next decision Dec 10

scenarios.base: If war fears stay at today's level, the franc holds near 0.82 per dollar.
scenarios.bull: If strikes on Iran or Gulf oil sites happen, safe-haven buying lifts the franc further.
scenarios.bear: If fear fades and carry trades return, the franc softens.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The Australian dollar ended flat near 70.2 US cents, recovering its morning dip as the US dollar eased, even as stocks fell. Coming up: Australia's flash business surveys at 5:00 PM CT tonight; markets still see close to even odds of a November rate hike.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Australia's inflation has picked up with energy prices, and Reserve Bank of Australia deputy governor Andrew Hauser said this week the outlook was materially worse, lifting the Australian dollar to a three-week high. What changed: no Australian news today. The Aussie dipped to about 0.7005 in the morning as stocks fell on Iran strike reports, then recovered to about 0.7017 as US yields dropped and the US dollar softened. The yen gained on it. What it means: rising hike bets keep the Aussie supported against the US dollar, but it still lags the safe havens when investors turn nervous. The question: does Australia's third-quarter inflation on October 28 settle the November decision?
chapters.fx: What's next: Australia's flash business surveys at 5:00 PM CT tonight. October 28: third-quarter consumer prices, the key input. November 2–3: the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision.

scenarios.bull: If tonight's business surveys are strong and stocks recover, November hike bets rise and the Aussie regains its high.
scenarios.bear: If the stock sell-off deepens on war and tech fears, the Aussie gives back its gains.

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The loonie edged up about 0.2% to near 1.403 per US dollar, helped by oil at its highest since May. Canada's factory and raw material prices jumped far more than expected, firming the case for a Bank of Canada hike next week.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: high oil lifts Canada's export income but also its inflation. Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said the bank's inflation forecast would be revised substantially higher on energy, and markets moved to expect a hike on October 28. What changed: Canada's industrial product prices, what factories charge, rose 2.0% in September (0.7% expected), and raw material prices rose 4.8% (0.1% expected). That is cost pressure building toward consumer prices. New home prices slipped 0.2%, a second soft month, a reminder that housing is cooling. US crude rose about 2.4% to near $99, and the US dollar eased to about 1.4031 Canadian. What it means: the October hike, already about 93% priced, looks even more justified, and the question shifts to whether more follow. The question: does the bank signal more hikes after October?
chapters.fx: What's next: Canadian retail sales for August at 7:30 AM CT Friday (about 1.3% expected after a 0.7% drop). October 28: the Bank of Canada's decision.
numbers: Factory-gate prices +2.0% m/m in Sep (0.7% expected); raw materials +4.8% (0.1% expected)

scenarios.bull: If oil climbs further or retail sales rebound strongly, bets on more hikes after October lift the loonie.
scenarios.bear: If oil falls on calmer Gulf news or stocks keep sliding, the loonie loses some support.

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: The kiwi fell about 0.5% to near 56.8 US cents, the weakest major currency today, as war fears and a tech sell-off hit stock markets. Markets still see a Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on October 28 as near certain.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: New Zealand's central bank, the RBNZ, has turned toward raising rates as energy and food push inflation above its 1–3% target band. Third-quarter inflation, out Wednesday evening, came in at 3.7%, a touch below forecasts but still above the band, and the hike stayed near fully priced. What changed: no new New Zealand news. The kiwi slid to about 0.5675 as reports of planned strikes on Iran and a sharp fall in US tech shares knocked stock markets, and it did not share in the afternoon recovery of the Australian dollar. What it means: the expected hike supports the kiwi, but it falls when investors get nervous. The question: does the RBNZ signal more than one hike when it meets?
chapters.fx: What's next: no major New Zealand data before the RBNZ's decision on October 28. Until then the kiwi moves with stock markets and the US dollar.

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Brent crude rose about 4% to near $113 a barrel, its highest since May, after the New York Times reported US and Israeli plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterms. US crude ended near $99.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: oil has been high since the US–Iran war began in February, with Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, largely shut. On Wednesday the US ordered some diplomats and families out of Saudi Arabia after deadly Houthi attacks. What changed: the New York Times reported that US and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans for a short but intense round of strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterms; President Trump has not approved them. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they hit four tankers in the Gulf and that three ships struck mines, claims not independently confirmed. Brent climbed through the day to about $113, and US crude to about $99. What it means: a renewed US campaign would put more Gulf supply at risk, so the risk premium in oil is rising. That feeds inflation worries and helps oil exporters like Canada, while hurting importers like Japan and the euro area. The question: do attacks reach actual oil output?
chapters.fx: What's next: any official US or Iranian response to the strike-plan report, and further attacks on Gulf shipping or Saudi oil sites. The Federal Reserve's decision on October 28 and the November 3 US midterms are the next fixed dates.
numbers: Iran's claims: 4 tankers hit, 3 ships struck mines (unconfirmed)

scenarios.bull: If an attack damages Gulf oil output or Hormuz traffic stops entirely, Brent climbs well above its May highs.
scenarios.bear: If Washington plays down the strike report or talks with Iran restart, Brent slips back toward $108.

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: Gold fell about 2.5% to near $4,045 an ounce, its fifth straight daily drop and a one-month low. It slid even as war fears rose and US yields fell, two things that usually help it.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: gold ran to records this year on war fears and central-bank buying, but it has slipped for a week as markets priced a December Federal Reserve hike, since gold pays no interest. What changed: gold fell to about $4,045, down for a fifth day, as reports of planned strikes on Iran pushed oil higher and stocks lower. Early in the day, market reports put the drop down to fears that oil-driven inflation keeps rate hikes coming. Gold kept falling in the afternoon even as US yields dropped sharply. What it means: neither war risk nor lower yields is lifting gold for now, so the slide looks driven by selling rather than by any one piece of news. Hedge funds were still strongly betting on gold in the latest US futures data, though trimming. The question: what finally breaks the slide, a real escalation or a lasting fall in rate-hike bets?
chapters.fx: What's next: Friday's US business surveys at 8:45 AM CT and the University of Michigan's inflation expectations at 9:00 AM CT, and any confirmed strike on Iran or Gulf oil sites. New US positioning data come Friday afternoon.

scenarios.bear: If Friday's US data firm the December Fed hike and yields recover, gold extends its slide below $4,000.

calls.text: France's revenue-section budget vote Tue: a clean pass narrows the French–German spread (~141bp); a defeat or big concessions widens it and weighs on the euro
calls.note: No vote on Tuesday: it was pushed to October 27, so neither branch played out.

calls.text: UK jobs Tue 1 AM CT (earnings ~3.8% expected): sticky pay firms the BoE hike case before Wednesday's inflation; cooling pay backs Bailey's calmer view
calls.note: Sticky side won: unemployment fell to 4.7% (4.9% expected) and regular pay rose 3.7% (3.6% expected); total pay and claims were softer. Pound +0.3% to ~1.334.

calls.text: Konarak follow-through: a US confirmation or more strikes keeps oil's supply premium and lifts US yields; silence lets the morning's waiver drop resume
calls.note: No confirmation (a US official denied the strike) and no new strike overnight, yet the premium held: Brent ~$109.8 Tuesday on low Gulf flows and Iran's Hormuz claims. The waiver-driven drop did not resume.

calls.text: BoC Oct 28 with ~87% priced for a hike: a hike is mostly in the loonie already; a hold would be the surprise and hit it
NZ Q3 CPI Wed 4:45pm CT (~3.8% y/y): near forecast keeps the ~80% hike pricing; clearly soft reopens the hold and weighs on the kiwi
calls.note: Near forecast (3.7% vs 3.8%) and hike pricing held, rising to about 98%; the kiwi dipped only briefly.
